title: Windows and Linux Logging for Detection
subtitle: Configuring and Analyzing OS Logs for Threat Detection
learning_objectives: Configure Windows Event Logs and Sysmon for comprehensive visibility
Set up Linux logging with syslog, auditd, and journald
Identify key log sources and event IDs critical for threat detection
Implement log enrichment strategies to improve detection quality
Troubleshoot common logging gaps and misconfigurations

content_blocks.title: Logging: Your Eyes on the Battlefield

content.text: Logging is the foundation of every detection program. You can't detect what you can't see. The most sophisticated detection logic is useless if the logs it needs don't exist. This lesson is about building that foundation — making sure you have the right logs, from the right places, with the right detail. Think of it as installing cameras before you start watching for intruders.

content_blocks.simplified_explanation: Logs are like security cameras. Before you can catch a thief, you need cameras in the right places pointing at the right things. This lesson teaches you where to put the cameras and how to make sure they're recording.
memory_aids: No logs = No detection = You're blind
Logs before logic — always
content_blocks.real_world_connection: In every major breach investigation, one of the first findings is insufficient logging. SolarWinds, MOVEit, the Uber breach — all had logging gaps that delayed detection by weeks or months.
content_blocks.reflection_prompt: How confident are you that your organization's logging covers the key detection scenarios?

content_blocks.title: Windows Event Log Architecture

content.text:
Windows provides several log channels, each serving different purposes:

**Core Security Log — Security.evtx**
- Authentication events (4624, 4625)
- Authorization changes (4670, 4713)
- Account management (4720, 4726, 4728, 4732)
- Policy changes (4670, 4719)
- Log clear events (1102)

**System Log — System.evtx**
- Service installations (7045)
- Driver loads (7036)
- System time changes (1)

**Application Log — Application.evtx**
- Application errors and crashes
- Custom application events

**PowerShell Logs**
- Script block logging (4104)
- Module logging (4103)
- Transcription logging

**Key Configuration Steps:**
```powershell
# Enable PowerShell Script Block Logging
reg add HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\ScriptBlockLogging \
  /v EnableScriptBlockLogging /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f

# Enable PowerShell Transcription
reg add HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\Transcription \
  /v EnableTranscripting /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f

# Increase Security log size to 4GB
wevtutil sl Security /ms:4294967296
```

content_blocks.simplified_explanation: Windows has multiple log 'books.' The Security log is your most important book — it records who logged in, who changed permissions, who created accounts. PowerShell logs are crucial because attackers love PowerShell.
memory_aids: Security.evtx = The main security camera
4624 = Successful login | 4625 = Failed login
PowerShell 4104 = Script block logging = See what scripts actually do
content_blocks.real_world_connection: PowerShell is the #1 tool for post-exploitation. Without script block logging (Event ID 4104), you'll only see that PowerShell ran — not what it actually executed. This is the single most important logging configuration for Windows detection.

content_blocks.title: Sysmon: The Detection Engineer's Best Friend

content.text:
Sysmon (System Monitor) is a Windows system service and device driver that provides detailed process creation, network connections, and file creation tracking. It's the single most important tool for Windows detection.

**Essential Sysmon Event IDs:**

| Event ID | What It Captures | Detection Value |
|----------|-----------------|-----------------|
| 1 | Process Creation | Command-line logging, parent-child relationships |
| 3 | Network Connection | C2 beaconing, lateral movement |
| 7 | Image Loaded (DLL) | DLL sideloading, injection |
| 8 | CreateRemoteThread | Process injection |
| 10 | Process Access | Credential theft (LSASS access) |
| 11 | File Create | Dropper detection |
| 13 | Registry Value Set | Persistence mechanisms |
| 22 | DNS Query | C2 domain resolution |
| 25 | Process Tampering | Process hollowing |

**Installing and Configuring Sysmon:**
```powershell
# Download Sysmon from Sysinternals
# Install with SwiftOnSecurity's config (excellent starting point)
Sysmon64.exe -accepteula -i sysmonconfig.xml

# Or install with Microsoft's recommended config
Sysmon64.exe -accepteula -i

# Verify installation
Get-WinEvent -LogName "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational" -MaxEvents 5
```

**SwiftOnSecurity Config Highlights:**
- Logs process creation with full command lines
- Logs all network connections
- Logs DNS queries
- Filters out noise (legitimate system processes)
- Logs DLL loads for suspicious locations
- Logs raw access reads (for credential access detection)

content_blocks.simplified_explanation: Sysmon is like a super-powered security camera that records every program startup, every network connection, every file creation, and every DNS lookup. Without it, you're flying blind on Windows.
memory_aids: Sysmon EID 1 = Process Creation (who ran what)
Sysmon EID 3 = Network Connection (who called home)
Sysmon EID 22 = DNS Query (what domain was looked up)
SwiftOnSecurity config = Best starting point
content_blocks.real_world_connection: Every major Windows detection rule in Sigma relies on Sysmon data. MITRE ATT&CK mapping for Windows techniques heavily depends on Sysmon events. Without Sysmon, you lose visibility into ~60% of ATT&CK techniques.
content_blocks.reflection_prompt: Is Sysmon deployed in your environment? If not, what's the first event ID you'd want to enable?

content_blocks.title: Linux Logging: syslog, auditd, and journald

content.text:
Linux provides three primary logging systems, each with different strengths:

**1. syslog / rsyslog**
The traditional Linux logging daemon. Captures system messages, kernel logs, and application output.

Key log files:
- `/var/log/auth.log` (Debian) or `/var/log/secure` (RHEL) — Authentication events
- `/var/log/syslog` (Debian) or `/var/log/messages` (RHEL) — General system logs
- `/var/log/kern.log` — Kernel messages
- `/var/log/cron` — Cron job execution

**2. auditd — The Linux Audit Framework**
For security-focused logging. auditd provides detailed tracking of system calls, file access, and security events.

```bash
# Key audit rules for security monitoring
# Track execve calls (process creation)
-a exit,always -F arch=b64 -S execve

# Track /etc/passwd modifications
-w /etc/passwd -p wa -k identity

# Track sudo usage
-w /etc/sudoers -p wa -k sudo_changes

# Track SSH key modifications
-w /root/.ssh/ -p wa -k ssh_keys

# Track cron modifications
-w /etc/cron* -p wa -k cron_changes
```

**3. journald (systemd)**
Modern logging system that stores logs in a binary format and provides powerful querying.

```bash
# Key journal commands
journalctl -u sshd                    # SSH daemon logs
journalctl -u auditd                  # Audit daemon logs
journalctl --since "1 hour ago"       # Recent logs
journalctl -p err                     # Error priority and above
journalctl -f                         # Follow (like tail -f)
```

**Recommended Configuration:**
- Enable auditd with process creation logging
- Forward all logs to a centralized SIEM
- Set appropriate log rotation and retention
- Use journald for ad-hoc investigation
- Configure rsyslog to forward to remote syslog server

content_blocks.simplified_explanation: Linux has three main logging tools: syslog (general system logs), auditd (security-focused tracking), and journald (modern, searchable logs). You need all three for complete visibility.
memory_aids: syslog = General logs (who, what, when)
auditd = Security camera (process creation, file changes, system calls)
journald = Modern search engine for logs
auth.log = Login attempts on Linux
content_blocks.real_world_connection: Linux servers are often overlooked in logging programs focused on Windows. But cloud infrastructure runs primarily on Linux, and Linux logging gaps are routinely exploited by attackers who know most organizations have weaker Linux visibility.

content_blocks.title: Log Enrichment with GeoIP and Threat Intelligence

content.text:
Raw logs are useful, but enriched logs are powerful. Here's how to enrich authentication logs with GeoIP and threat intel data:

```python
import geoip2.database
import json
from datetime import datetime

def enrich_auth_event(event, geoip_db, threat_intel):
    """Enrich an authentication event with geo and threat intel."""
    enriched = event.copy()
    
    # GeoIP enrichment
    try:
        response = geoip_db.city(event.get('source_ip', ''))
        enriched['geo'] = {
            'country': response.country.iso_code,
            'city': response.city.name,
            'latitude': response.location.latitude,
            'longitude': response.location.longitude,
            'isp': response.traits.isp
        }
    except:
        enriched['geo'] = {'country': 'Unknown', 'city': 'Unknown'}
    
    # Threat intel enrichment
    source_ip = event.get('source_ip', '')
    if source_ip in threat_intel.get('malicious_ips', set()):
        enriched['threat_intel'] = {
            'malicious': True,
            'source': 'threat_feed',
            'tags': threat_intel['malicious_ips'][source_ip]
        }
    
    # Risk scoring
    risk_score = 0
    if enriched.get('event_id') == '4625':  # Failed login
        risk_score += 10
    if enriched.get('logon_type') == 3:  # Network logon
        risk_score += 5
    if enriched.get('geo', {}).get('country') not in ['US', 'IL']:
        risk_score += 20
    if enriched.get('threat_intel', {}).get('malicious'):
        risk_score += 50
    
    enriched['risk_score'] = risk_score
    return enriched

# Example usage
event = {
    'event_id': '4625',
    'source_ip': '185.220.101.45',
    'username': 'admin',
    'logon_type': 3,
    'timestamp': '2026-06-21T14:30:00Z'
}

# In practice, load these from actual databases
# geoip_db = geoip2.database.Reader('GeoIP2-City.mmdb')
# threat_intel = load_threat_feed()
print(json.dumps(enrich_auth_event(event, None, {'malicious_ips': {}}), indent=2))
```

content_blocks.simplified_explanation: Raw logs tell you WHAT happened. Enriched logs tell you WHY it matters. Adding country, threat intel, and risk scores turns 'failed login from IP X' into 'failed login from known malicious Russian IP with high risk score.'
memory_aids: Raw log = WHAT | Enriched log = WHY IT MATTERS
GeoIP + Threat Intel + Risk Score = Detection gold
content_blocks.real_world_connection: SIEM platforms like Splunk and Microsoft Sentinel perform this enrichment automatically, but understanding the process helps you design better detection rules and validate enrichment quality.

content_blocks.title: Logging Gaps That Cost Months of Detection Time

content.text:
**Case Study: The Missing PowerShell Logs**

An organization was compromised for 87 days before detection. The attacker used PowerShell extensively for lateral movement and data collection. Investigation revealed:

**What Was Missing:**
1. PowerShell Script Block Logging was not enabled — only saw `powershell.exe` in process logs, not the actual commands
2. Sysmon was not deployed on 40% of endpoints — no process creation or network connection data
3. Linux auth.log was only retained for 7 days — attacker's initial SSH brute force was already overwritten
4. auditd was not configured for process creation — no visibility into commands executed via SSH

**What This Cost:**
- 87 days of dwell time
- $2.3M in incident response costs
- Regulatory fines for insufficient logging
- Lost customer trust

**Remediation:**
1. Deployed Sysmon with SwiftOnSecurity config to all endpoints
2. Enabled PowerShell Script Block Logging via GPO
3. Extended Linux log retention to 90 days
4. Configured auditd with comprehensive process creation rules
5. Forwarded all logs to SIEM with 1-year hot storage

**Detection Gap Cost Formula:**
`Detection_Time = Time_Without_Logs + Investigation_Time`
`Cost = Detection_Time × Data_Exfiltration_Rate + IR_Cost + Regulatory_Fines`

content_blocks.simplified_explanation: Missing logs = blind spots = longer breach detection time. The organization couldn't see PowerShell commands, couldn't see process creation on 40% of machines, and overwrote Linux logs too quickly. Each gap added weeks to detection time.
memory_aids: 87 days dwell time because of 4 logging gaps
PowerShell without script block logging = seeing a gun, not seeing the bullet
content_blocks.real_world_connection: This pattern repeats across breach reports. The most common gaps: no Sysmon, no PowerShell logging, insufficient retention, no Linux auditd. Fix these four and you'll cover ~80% of common detection needs.

content_blocks.title: OS Logging Essentials Cheat Sheet

content.text:
**Windows Logging Essentials:**

📋 **Must-Have Windows Event IDs:**
| ID | Description | Detection Use |
|-----|------------|-------------- |
| 4624 | Successful logon | Login tracking |
| 4625 | Failed logon | Brute force detection |
| 4648 | Explicit credential logon | Lateral movement |
| 4672 | Special privileges | Privilege escalation |
| 4720 | User created | Persistence |
| 4732 | Member added to group | Privilege escalation |
| 7045 | Service installed | Persistence |
| 1102 | Audit log cleared | Anti-forensics |

🔧 **Sysmon Critical Event IDs:**
| ID | Description |
|-----|------------|
| 1 | Process Creation |
| 3 | Network Connection |
| 7 | Image Loaded (DLL) |
| 8 | CreateRemoteThread |
| 10 | Process Access |
| 22 | DNS Query |

🐧 **Linux Logging Commands:**
- `auditd`: Process execution, file changes, SSH key mods
- `auth.log/secure`: Authentication events
- `journalctl -u <service>`: Service-specific logs
- `/var/log/syslog`: General system logs

memory_aids: 4624 = Good login | 4625 = Bad login | 4648 = Using someone's creds
Sysmon 1=Process 3=Network 22=DNS
Linux: auditd for security, auth.log for logins, journald for ad-hoc

content_blocks.title: Log Collection and Forwarding Architecture

content.text:
Getting logs from endpoints to your SIEM requires a robust collection architecture:

**Windows Log Collection:**
- **WinLogBeat** (Elastic): Lightweight, configurable, good for Elastic Stack
- **Splunk Universal Forwarder**: For Splunk environments
- **Azure Monitor Agent**: For Microsoft Sentinel
- **NXLog**: Flexible, supports multiple outputs

**Linux Log Collection:**
- **Filebeat/Auditbeat** (Elastic): Syslog + auditd + journald
- **Splunk Universal Forwarder**: For Splunk environments
- **rsyslog remote forwarding**: Simple, built-in
- **Fluentd/Fluent Bit**: Lightweight, cloud-native

**Architecture Best Practices:**

```
[Endpoints] → [Log Forwarders] → [Log Aggregator] → [SIEM]
     ↓                                    ↓
[Local Buffer]                    [Log Rotation]
```

**Key Design Decisions:**
1. **Local buffering**: Always buffer logs locally before forwarding to prevent data loss
2. **TLS encryption**: All log forwarding must use TLS
3. **Load balancing**: Use multiple aggregators behind a load balancer
4. **Log format normalization**: Normalize before or during ingestion
5. **Retention policy**: Hot storage (searchable) 90+ days, cold storage 1+ year
6. **Compression**: Enable on forwarders to reduce bandwidth

content_blocks.simplified_explanation: Log collection is like a plumbing system. Every endpoint is a faucet, the log forwarders are pipes, the aggregator is a water tank, and the SIEM is the treatment plant. If any pipe is clogged or missing, you lose visibility.
memory_aids: Endpoints → Forwarders → Aggregator → SIEM
Always encrypt (TLS), always buffer locally, always plan for scale
content_blocks.real_world_connection: A common failure mode is log forwarders going down silently. Without local buffering, logs are lost. Without monitoring the forwarders themselves, you have a gap you don't even know about.

content_blocks.title: Key Takeaways and Self-Assessment

content.text:
**Quick self-check — can you answer these?**

1. **Why is Sysmon critical for Windows detection?**
   — It provides process creation (EID 1), network connections (EID 3), DNS queries (EID 22), and other events not available in standard Windows logs.

2. **What's the most important PowerShell logging to enable?**
   — Script Block Logging (EID 4104) — it captures the actual PowerShell code executed, not just `powershell.exe`.

3. **What's the Linux equivalent of Sysmon for process creation?**
   — auditd with an execve system call rule (`-a exit,always -F arch=b64 -S execve`).

4. **What are the three pillars of log enrichment?**
   — GeoIP enrichment, threat intelligence enrichment, and risk scoring.

5. **Why must log forwarders use local buffering?**
   — To prevent log loss when the network or aggregator is unavailable.

content_blocks.reflection_prompt: Which of these logging gaps exist in your current environment? What would you fix first?

content_blocks.title: Logging is the Foundation

content.text:
You've now learned how to configure and collect the logs that feed every detection, investigation, and response action. Remember: the best detection rules in the world are useless without the right logs to feed them.

**Key Principles:**
1. **Deploy before you need it** — Logging after an incident is too late
2. **Sysmon + PowerShell logging is non-negotiable for Windows**
3. **auditd + auth.log is non-negotiable for Linux**
4. **Enrichment turns raw logs into detection fuel**
5. **Buffer locally, forward securely, retain wisely**

Every minute without proper logging is a minute an attacker can operate invisibly. Build the foundation first, then the detection logic will have fuel to run on.

memory_aids: Logs before logic — always
Sysmon + PowerShell on Windows, auditd + auth.log on Linux
Deploy logging BEFORE the incident, not after

post_assessment.question: Which Windows logging feature is most critical for detecting PowerShell-based attacks?
post_assessment.explanation: Script Block Logging (EID 4104) captures the actual PowerShell code being executed, not just the process name. This is essential because attackers heavily use PowerShell, and without script block logging you only see `powershell.exe` ran, not what it actually did.

post_assessment.question: What is the primary purpose of Sysmon Event ID 1 (Process Creation)?
options: To log when a system service starts
To record detailed information about new processes including full command lines and parent process relationships
post_assessment.explanation: Sysmon EID 1 logs process creation with full command lines, parent process information, hashes of the executable, and the user context. This is the foundation of endpoint detection — seeing exactly what ran, how it was invoked, and by which parent process.

post_assessment.question: Which Linux logging tool is specifically designed for security event tracking, including system calls like execve?
post_assessment.explanation: auditd is the Linux Audit Daemon, specifically designed for security-focused logging. It can track system calls (like execve for process creation), file modifications, and security events. rsyslog and journald capture general system messages, but auditd provides the granular security tracking equivalent to Sysmon on Windows.

post_assessment.question: Why is local buffering important for log forwarders?
options: It prevents log loss when the network or centralized aggregator is unavailable
It compresses logs to save disk space
It filters out unimportant log entries
post_assessment.explanation: Local buffering ensures that if the log aggregator or network connection goes down, logs are stored locally and can be forwarded once connectivity is restored. Without buffering, any logs generated during an outage are permanently lost — creating detection gaps.

post_assessment.question: What are the three main pillars of log enrichment for threat detection?
options: GeoIP enrichment, threat intelligence enrichment, and risk scoring
post_assessment.explanation: GeoIP enrichment adds location context (where is this IP?), threat intelligence adds threat context (is this IP malicious?), and risk scoring adds priority context (how suspicious is this event?). Together, they transform raw logs into actionable detection data.
